input: The schedule float for the upgrade project has been set at 16%, and the figure has been questioned on the ground that a lower allowance would present a tighter and more ambitious programme. That argument is understandable, but it overlooks what the float is there to do. The float is not spare time added for comfort; it is the allowance that stands between the planned sequence of work and the point at which slippage in one activity begins to consume the dates of the activities that follow it. Several of the activities on the critical path have durations that cannot be fixed with precision at this stage, because they depend on interfaces between work packages and on approval steps that lie outside the direct control of the project team. If the float were set lower, the first significant slippage would exhaust the allowance, and every subsequent delay would move the completion date directly, leaving the steering group to recover time by compressing work that is already planned tightly. The cost consequences of such compression are set out in the cost table in the Costs section, and they are not repeated here; the point for the schedule is that recovery after the float has gone is bought at a price, whereas the float itself costs nothing until it is used. Retaining the stated figure keeps a single, visible allowance under the control of the steering group, rather than distributing hidden padding through individual activity durations, where it would be spent without being tracked. For those reasons the float should stay as set, and the steering group is asked to endorse the figure when the programme is reviewed.

Float is the allowance between the planned sequence of work and the point where slippage in one activity begins to consume the dates of the activities after it. Float is not spare time added for comfort. Several activities on the critical path have durations that cannot be fixed with precision at this stage. Critical-path activities depend on interfaces between work packages and on approval steps outside the direct control of the project team. A lower float is exhausted by the first significant slippage. Every later delay then moves the completion date directly, and the steering group must recover time by compressing work already planned tightly. The cost of such compression is set out in the cost table in the Costs section and is not repeated here. Recovery after the float has gone is bought at a price; the float itself costs nothing until it is used. A single visible allowance, held under the control of the steering group, is also easier to protect than padding distributed through individual activity durations, where allowance is spent without being tracked. The float stays as set, and the steering group is asked to endorse the figure at the programme review.

The defence of the figure is practical. Float that is visible can be allocated deliberately, activity by activity, as risks materialise. Float that has been designed out cannot be recovered except by compression of the work or by movement of the completion date, and both routes are decided under pressure, after slippage has already occurred.
